Since the 1960s it has become a commercialized pan-Indian symbol, one scholars caution has drifted from its original use.
source: Ojibwe oral tradition and early ethnographic accounts

name: Calumet (Peace Pipe)
material: Stone bowl and wood stem, sometimes catlinite
powers: Binds treaties, prayers and peace in a single sacred act.
description: The sacred pipe of Plains peoples, its stone bowl and wood stem smoked in ceremonies of prayer, treaty and peace; in Lakota tradition the chanunpa was given to the people by White Buffalo Calf Woman. The name 'calumet' comes from French via early traders who witnessed its power to seal alliances. Carved catlinite bowls, the pipestone of Minnesota, are among the most famous examples.
source: Lakota oral tradition and early French accounts

name: Wampum Belt
material: Quahog and whelk shell beads woven into belts
era: Eastern Woodlands tradition to the present
powers: Records treaties and laws in a living web of shell.
description: Belts woven from purple and white shell beads that served Eastern Woodlands peoples, especially the Haudenosaunee, as records of treaties, laws and historic events; the patterns carried the meaning read aloud at councils. The Great Law of Peace and the Hiawatha belt are among the most celebrated. Colonists adopted wampum as trade currency, a role that reshaped but never erased its ceremonial use.
source: Haudenosaunee oral tradition and colonial records

name: Kachina Doll
material: Carved cottonwood root with paint and feathers
powers: Brings the blessing of the katsinam spirits to children.
description: Small carved and painted wooden figures of the katsinam, the spirit messengers of the Hopi, given to children to teach the identity and power of each being that visits the village from winter to summer. Carved from cottonwood root, the dolls are educational rather than worshipped, yet carry sacred meaning and ceremony. Since the late 1800s they have also become celebrated art sought by museums.
source: Hopi oral tradition and ethnographic studies

name: Medicine Bag
era: Indigenous North America to the present
powers: Holds the personal medicines given to its owner in a dream.
description: A small hide pouch carried or kept privately, holding the personal medicines, feathers, stones and charms revealed to its owner in vision or dream across many North American nations. The contents are personal and often secret, and the bag's power depends on how faithfully its owner follows the vision. Ethnographic accounts note it is never opened lightly and is buried with its owner.
source: Plains and Woodlands oral tradition and ethnography

name: False Face Mask
material: Carved basswood with red and black paint
powers: Wards off sickness with the power of the forest spirits.
description: A distorted human face carved from living basswood, painted red and black, used by the Haudenosaunee False Face Society in curing ceremonies that drive sickness away. The twisted faces recall the forest being who broke his face in a contest with the sun and gained power over disease. Sacred, handled only by society members, the masks are cut from the living tree without metal.

name: Yeibichai Mask
material: Painted buckskin with feathers and turquoise
powers: Lets a dancer embody a Holy Person in ceremony.
description: The painted buckskin mask worn by Navajo dancers so they may embody the Holy People (ye'i) in the great nightway ceremonies, healing rites whose chants invoke Changing Woman and the blessing of the gods. Made anew for each ceremony and used only by initiated singers, the masks are never sold or displayed, and carry the marks that identify each Holy Person to the community.
source: Navajo oral tradition and ceremonial practice

name: Birchbark Canoe
material: Birchbark over cedar frame with spruce root lashing
powers: Glides silently over lakes and rivers, light enough to carry.
description: The light, silent canoe built of birchbark sewn over a cedar frame with spruce root, the great carrier of the Anishinaabe and other northern peoples across lakes and portages. A single canoe could be carried by one person and moved across hundreds of miles of waterways, which is why traders and explorers adopted it. Master builders still construct it with the same bark, gum and root joinery.
source: Anishinaabe oral tradition and historical accounts

name: Cedar Bark Basket
culture: Haida, Tlingit and other Northwest Coast peoples
era: Northwest Coast tradition to the present
powers: Holds water itself when woven tight enough.
description: Baskets and hats woven from shredded cedar bark and split cedar root by the women of the Northwest Coast, some so tightly made they can hold water and be used for cooking with hot stones. The weaving carries the distinctive twined patterns of each nation, from simple checks to complex animal designs. Cedar itself is the subject of origin stories tying its use to the forest's generosity.
source: Northwest Coast oral tradition and ethnographic collections

name: Totem Pole
era: Northwest Coast tradition to the present
powers: Proclaims clan lineage and stories in carved cedar.
description: Towering poles carved from whole cedar trunks by Northwest Coast peoples, raised before houses to proclaim lineage, honor the dead, or tell the stories of founding ancestors and the beings who helped them. The figures are not idols but crests and histories, read by those who know them. Colonial bans interrupted carving; the art revived in the twentieth century as a symbol of regional identity.
source: Northwest Coast oral tradition and historical accounts

name: Thunderbird Club
powers: Carries the strike of the thunderbird into battle.
description: A heavy carved club whose grip and head are shaped as a bird, most often the thunderbird, so that each blow falls with the power of the being who makes the thunder and carries lightning. Carried by chiefs and warriors, the club combines weapon and emblem, its carved beak and wings binding the bearer to the great sky bird of the origin stories. Surviving examples are treasured in museums.
source: Northwest Coast and Plains oral tradition

name: Coup Stick
culture: Plains peoples (Lakota, Cheyenne, Crow and others)
powers: Touching the enemy is the highest act of bravery.
description: A staff or lance carried by Plains warriors to 'count coup,' touching an enemy in battle without killing being regarded as the bravest feat of all. Eagle feathers and scalps added to the staff record each coup the bearer counted, a living tally of honor. Ethnographic accounts record that the four highest honors of Plains warfare were ranked, with counting coup above taking an enemy's life.

name: War Bonnet
culture: Plains peoples (Lakota, Cheyenne, Blackfoot and others)
material: Eagle feathers on a hide cap or band
powers: Each feather marks an honor earned in war or ceremony.
description: The grand headdress of upright eagle feathers worn by Plains chiefs, each feather earned by bravery or a vision and the whole assembled with ceremony. The straight-up bonnet familiar from photographs became prominent in the nineteenth century; earlier forms differed widely. Feathers could also be earned for deeds in peace, and the bonnet is worn with respect as a symbol of leadership.
source: Plains oral tradition and historical accounts

name: Medicine Wheel
material: Arranged stones in a circle with spokes
era: From at least the late prehistoric era
powers: Mirrors the four directions and the circle of life.
description: Circles of stones laid out with radiating spokes on the high plains, the most famous in the Bighorn Mountains of Wyoming, whose alignment some studies tie to the solstices. The wheel is read as a sacred model of the cosmos, the four directions, the seasons and the human journey, a teaching that continues among Plains nations. The purpose of the oldest sites remains a matter of debate.
source: Plains oral tradition and archaeological study

name: Katsina Owl Doll
powers: Teaches children the ways of the night hunter spirit.
description: A carved and painted doll of the owl katsina, one of the Hopi spirit beings that return to the villages in season, given to children so they learn the owl's wisdom and hunting power. Like other katsina tihu the doll is made of cottonwood root, its wings and face marked in the colors of the specific spirit. It belongs to the katsina carvings that carry the ceremonies' teaching into the home.
source: Hopi oral tradition and ethnographic studies

name: Three Sisters Garden
culture: Haudenosaunee and other Eastern Woodlands peoples
material: Interplanted corn, beans and squash in mounds
powers: The three crops support each other as the sisters did the people.
description: The Haudenosaunee method of planting corn, beans and squash together in one mound, each crop helping the others: corn gives the beans a pole, beans fix the soil, and squash shades the roots. The three are called sisters in the peoples' stories, inseparable companions who arrived with the ancestors. The system fed the confederacy, and its lessons in companion planting are studied by farmers today.
source: Haudenosaunee oral tradition and agricultural history

name: Inukshuk
powers: Guides travelers and marks the good hunting ground.
description: Figures built of stacked stones by Inuit and other Arctic peoples, used as landmarks to guide travelers, mark good hunting or fishing places, or stand as memorials on the open tundra where there are no trees. The human-shaped inuksuk is best known from the flag of Nunavut, though most cairns were simple and practical. Each is a deliberate sign in a landscape that offers few bearings.
source: Inuit oral tradition and Arctic ethnographic records

name: Hex Sign
material: Painted wooden or tin barn disk
powers: Wards off harm and invites luck on the barn.
description: The painted circles and stars fixed to Pennsylvania Dutch barns, bright patterns of tulips, hearts and eight-point stars read as charms for luck and protection, although 'hex' in this sense meant 'spell' to outsiders. Fraktur and folk-art records show the motifs rooted in the German settlers of the 1700s. Scholars note the protective meanings are partly popular belief layered over decoration.
source: Pennsylvania Dutch folk art and regional studies

name: Jack-o'-Lantern
material: Carved hollow pumpkin with a candle
era: Irish tradition; American form since the 19th century
powers: Keeps the wandering soul of Jack at bay with its light.
description: A hollowed pumpkin carved with a face and lit from inside, placed on porches at Halloween, the American descendant of the Irish turnip lantern of 'Stingy Jack.' In the legend the trickster Jack, barred from heaven and hell, walks the dark carrying a coal in a carved turnip, called jack-o'-lantern after him. Irish immigrants carried the tale to America, where the pumpkin replaced the turnip.

name: Gris-Gris Bag
material: Red flannel pouch with herbs, roots, coins or stones
era: From the colonial era to the present
powers: Carries the working of the root doctor for love, luck or protection.
description: A small flannel pouch filled with herbs, roots, stones or personal items, made by Louisiana root doctors and hoodoo practitioners to carry a working for love, luck, money or protection; gris-gris is the name used in New Orleans, mojo in other regions. The practice blends African spiritual traditions with colonial folk belief. Bags are carried on the body and often must be fed to take effect.
source: Louisiana hoodoo tradition and ethnographic records

name: Haint Blue Paint
material: Pale blue-green paint, traditionally with indigo or lime
era: From the colonial era to the present
powers: Keeps haints, the wandering spirits, from entering the house.
description: The pale blue paint used on porch ceilings, doors and window frames of the Gullah Lowcountry of the Carolinas and Georgia, said to keep haints, the restless spirits of the dead, from entering the house. Water is the traditional veil between the living and the dead, and the blue is read as its color, though some note practical roots in lime and indigo. The practice continues beyond the Lowcountry.
source: Gullah oral tradition and regional studies

name: Witch Bottle
material: Stoneware or glass bottle with pins, nails, hair and urine
powers: Traps the witch's harm and turns it back on her.
description: A bottle packed with pins, nails, hair and sometimes urine, sealed and hidden in a wall, chimney or hearth to draw a witch's spell into itself and break it, a practice brought from Europe to colonial America. Scores of bottles have been found bricked into old American and English buildings. The charm offers the bottle as a decoy and a trap, its sharp contents meant to wound the witch in return.
source: Colonial American folk magic and archaeological finds

name: Sweetgrass Basket
era: From the colonial era to the present
powers: Carries the memory of African weaving in every coil.
description: Coiled baskets woven from sweetgrass and palmetto leaf by Gullah weavers of the Lowcountry, a craft brought to America from West Africa and continued on the rice coast for three centuries. The tight coil stitch is nearly unchanged from African prototypes, and the baskets long served in rice processing before becoming prized art. The tradition survives in Mount Pleasant and the Sea Islands.
source: Gullah weaving tradition and cultural studies

name: Kero
material: Carved wood, often with painted scenes
powers: Twin cups shared to seal alliance and honor the sun.
description: The paired ceremonial cups of the Andes, carved from wood as a flared goblet and drunk from in pairs at rituals of alliance, hospitality and the great festivals of the Inca calendar. Drunk together so each party shared the other's drink, twin keros sealed friendship. Colonial-era keros are painted with scenes of Inca life, a key record of how the empire remembered itself after conquest.
source: Inca-period and colonial keros in museum collections

name: Tumi
powers: Sacrificial blade of the priests under the moon.
description: The tumi is the crescent-bladed ceremonial knife of the Andes, a wide arched gold blade on a decorated handle, crafted by the Lambayeque/Sicán culture and later carried into Inca ritual and sacrifice. The most famous example, the Tumi of Lambayeque, was found at Batán Grande in 1936 and has become a national symbol of Peru, reproduced in folk art and worn as an emblem of identity.
source: Lambayeque/Sicán and Inca archaeological finds, including the Tumi of Lambayeque (1936)

name: Quipu
material: Colored and knotted cotton or camelid cords
era: Andean tradition to the colonial era
powers: Records numbers, tribute and histories in knots.
description: A system of knotted cords used across the Andes to record numbers, tribute, calendars and, many scholars believe, narrative information; the Inca kept archives for the empire's accounts. A main cord hangs subsidiary cords whose colors, positions and knots encode data, read by the khipu-kamayuq. Spanish chroniclers called them the 'books' of the empire, and they remain under active research.
source: Colonial chronicles and surviving Inca quipus

name: Mama Cocha Effigy
powers: Gains the protection of the mother of the sea.
description: Small images and offerings made to Mama Cocha, the mother of the sea, honored by the Inca for the fish, shells and travel she provided along the Pacific coast. Fisherfolk made offerings of shell and stone at the shore, and colonial accounts record the goddess among the household and regional deities the Inca honored. The amulets carry her power out to the boats that worked her waters.
source: Colonial chronicles of Inca religion and coastal offerings

name: Pachamanca
material: Heated stones dug into the earth
powers: Feeds the community and returns its first taste to the earth.
description: The Andean feast cooked by heating stones in a pit and steaming meat, potatoes, maize and herbs above them, its name meaning 'earth pot.' The cooking is tied to the land itself, and the first portion is traditionally offered to Pachamama, the earth mother, before anyone eats. Pachamanca is still prepared across the Peruvian and Bolivian highlands for festivals, weddings and planting days.
source: Andean oral tradition and contemporary practice

name: Mate Gourd
era: From the colonial era to the present
powers: Shared in a circle that marks friendship and trust.
description: The dried gourd cup in which yerba mate, the leafy infusion of the Guaraní, is drunk through a metal straw, passed hand to hand in a fixed order among friends in Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay. The Guaraní drank the herb before the Spanish arrived, and sharing one gourd marks closeness; etiquette governs who pours and who drinks next. It remains the everyday companion of millions.
source: Guaraní tradition and colonial accounts of mate

name: Bolas
material: Balls of stone or iron joined by braided hide cords
era: From the colonial era to the present
powers: Entangles the legs of running cattle or game.
description: Two or three weights joined by braided cords, swung and hurled to wrap around the legs of fleeing cattle, horses or game, the signature hunting tool of the Argentine pampas and of the gaucho. The technique came to the region with the Indigenous peoples of the plains and was adopted wholesale by the colonial cattle herders. Versions were recorded among the Mapuche and other southern peoples.

name: Kultrún
powers: Carries the heartbeat of the land into ceremony.
description: The round drum of the Mapuche, its head painted with a cross and the four directions, struck by the machi, the ceremonial leader and healer, in rites and visions. Its beat paces the ngillatun ceremonies of thanks and the healing of the sick, and the drum is regarded as sacred, held in the machi's hands at the center of the ritual circle. The kultrún stands at the heart of Mapuche spiritual life.
source: Mapuche oral tradition and ethnographic studies

name: Rewe
material: Carved wooden post with notched steps
powers: Ladder by which the machi climbs to speak with the spirits.
description: The tall notched post raised at the center of Mapuche ceremonies, its steps climbed by the machi to draw close to the upper world of the spirits; the rewe marks the place where the sacred and human worlds meet. Each rewe is carved and planted with ceremony, often with images of the beings that guide the machi. It stands at the heart of the ngillatun ritual ground.
source: Mapuche oral tradition and ethnographic studies

name: Saci's Red Cap
aliases: The Cap of the One-Legged Imp
era: Brazilian folk tradition to the present
powers: Whoever wins it gains the Saci's power.
description: The red knitted cap worn by Saci, the one-legged mischief spirit of Brazilian folklore; to take it is to gain Saci's obedience or his magic, and tales tell of those who steal it only to lose it again. Saci is said to rest his spinning tricks and whistling when he sleeps, the cap beside him. The cap alone identifies him in folk art and story.
source: Brazilian oral tradition and Monteiro Lobato's tales

name: Supay Figurine
powers: Opens the door to the world beneath the earth.
description: Images and masks of Supay, the lord of the Andean underworld known as uku pacha, the world beneath the earth, honored and feared for his rule over the dead and the mountain's depths. In the colonial era his name was pressed into service for the devil, and festivals still carry the blurred figure, half ancient lord, half devil. His power is invoked at carnival and in the mines.
source: Andean oral tradition and colonial records

name: Pishtaco Knife
era: Andean folk belief to the present
powers: Cuts fat from the living to sell it in secret.
description: The blade of the Pishtaco, the feared figure of the Andes who is said to cut the fat from sleeping travelers and sell it, a belief rooted in the very real dread of the stranger in the highlands. Whistling in the dark or a shadow at the roadside is enough to raise the fear of the fat-stealer. The belief adapts, attaching to whoever the community fears most, from priests to gringos.
source: Andean folk belief and regional studies

name: Zemi (Taino Effigy)
material: Carved wood, stone, bone or cotton
powers: Houses a spirit and speaks through the behique.
description: Sculpted figures of the Taino holding a spirit, or zemi, carved from wood, stone or cotton and kept in the household or the cacique's house to give health, good harvests or answers through the behique (shaman). Spanish accounts record caciques who owned great numbers of them, and a few wooden examples survive. The word zemi names both the spirit and the object that houses it.
source: Colonial accounts and surviving Taino objects

name: Vejigante Mask
material: Papier-mâché with horns, fangs and bright colors
era: From the colonial era to the present
powers: Scares away evil with its horns and colors at carnival.
description: The fierce carnival masks of Ponce, Puerto Rico, with their horns, fangs, bulging eyes and wild colors, worn by the vejigante during Carnival to tease crowds and chase away evil spirits. The tradition mixes the Spanish celebration of the festival with African and Taino elements, each town with its own style. The mask is now both a carnival essential and a celebrated Puerto Rican folk art form.

name: Asson
material: Gourd rattle with snake vertebrae and beads
era: Haitian Vodou tradition to the present
powers: Rings the spirits into the peristyle at ceremony.
description: The rattle of Haitian Vodou, a gourd fitted with a handle and strung with snake vertebrae and beads, shaken by the houngan or mambo to summon the lwa into the peristyle (temple) at ceremonies. Only the priest or priestess handles it, and its shaking marks the moment the spirits arrive to possess the faithful. The asson is among the most sacred objects of Vodou ritual.
source: Haitian Vodou practice and ethnographic studies

name: Govi
era: Haitian Vodou tradition to the present
powers: Holds the spirits of the ancestors and the dead.
description: A clay jar or bottle used in Haitian Vodou to contain the presence of the dead or the spirits of the ancestors, kept in the temple and opened with care by the priest. The govi is an ordinary vessel made extraordinary by the ritual that fills it, and its handling is governed by strict rules of respect. It links the community of the living with the world beneath.
source: Haitian Vodou practice and ethnographic studies

name: Batá Drum
material: Carved hardwood with animal hide heads
era: Cuban Santería tradition to the present
powers: Talks the language of the orishas at ceremony.
description: The sacred twin drums of Cuban Santería, carved in an hourglass shape with heads of different sizes, played only by initiates in ceremonies where their rhythms are said to speak the language of the orishas. The drums descend from the Yoruba bata of West Africa, carried by enslaved people to Cuba and preserved behind Catholic saints. Each drum is consecrated and named when it is made.
source: Cuban Santería practice and music studies

name: Eleke
material: Beaded necklaces in the colors of the orishas
era: Cuban Santería tradition to the present
powers: Binds the wearer to the protection of a specific orisha.
description: The bead necklaces of Cuban Santería, each strung in the colors of a particular orisha and given in ceremony to mark the wearer under that spirit's protection. The eleke is consecrated and must be removed only with respect, and its colors reveal the orisha to those who know the tradition. It descends from the beaded collars of Yoruba religion and marks initiation and devotion.
source: Cuban Santería practice and ethnographic studies

name: Duho
powers: Raises the cacique above the ground and close to the spirits.
description: The duho is the carved wooden seat of the Taíno, a ceremonial stool of guaiacum or mahogany on which caciques sat in ritual, often carved as a creature or reclining zemi figure. Spanish chroniclers recorded chiefs receiving Columbus seated on duhos; museum-dated examples from about AD 600 span the islands from Cuba to the Bahamas. It raised its user toward the spirits in cohoba ceremonies.
source: Archaeological duhos in museum collections and early colonial accounts

name: Lechuguilla Mask
powers: Worn at the Fiestas de los Santos Inocentes to escape King Herod.
description: The masked costume of the Fiestas de los Santos Inocentes in Hatillo, Puerto Rico, where on December 28 masqueraders run through town in vejigante-style masks and painted gowns to re-enact King Herod's search for the Christ child. Brought by settlers from the Canary Islands in 1823, the mask lets the wearer hide from the story's soldiers and turn the day into a chase of laughter.

name: Qulliq
material: Carved soapstone with a moss or cotton wick
powers: The woman's light and warmth that held the igloo together.
description: The crescent-shaped soapstone lamp of the Inuit, burned with seal oil and a moss wick to warm the igloo, melt snow for water, and light the long Arctic night; the qulliq was tended by women and stood at the center of household life. One lamp heated the whole dwelling, and a well-trimmed wick marked a skilled housewife. The lamp is still lit at Inuit gatherings to honor the tradition.
source: Inuit oral tradition and Arctic ethnographic records

name: Ulu
material: Blade of iron or slate with wood, bone or antler handle
powers: The all-purpose blade of the household and the camp.
description: The broad curved blade of the Inuit and other Arctic peoples, held by a short handle and used for skinning, cutting meat, scraping hides, and preparing food; the ulu is primarily a woman's knife and a symbol of her household. Its shape let pressure be applied with the whole arm, cutting through thick hide and frozen meat alike. Modern steel ulus are still made and used in the North today.
source: Inuit tradition and Arctic ethnographic records

name: Kayak
material: Sealskin stretched over a wood or bone frame
powers: Carries its hunter silently across the open sea after seals.
description: The one-man hunting boat of the Inuit, a frame of wood or bone covered with sealskin, so light and watertight that one hunter could carry it and paddle it alone across the open sea after seals and whales. The hunter sat in its cockpit, its deck lashed tight against waves. European explorers copied its shape, and the kayak entered the world's boats as a living Arctic invention.
source: Inuit oral tradition and Arctic maritime records

name: Amauti
material: Caribou skin with a large back hood
powers: Carries a baby in warmth against its mother's back.
description: The woman's parka of the Inuit, cut with a large hood and a deep pouch across the back in which a baby rides warm against its mother's skin; the amauti is sewn of caribou skin by the women, who are famed for the accuracy of their cutting and stitching. The pouch lets the child nurse and sleep without being taken out into the cold. It is one of the most admired garments of the Arctic.
source: Inuit tradition and Arctic ethnographic records

name: Tupilak
material: Carved bone, ivory, antler or stone
powers: A vengeful spirit assembled to harm an enemy.
description: A figure the Greenlandic Inuit carved from bone, skin or other gathered parts and animated with magic to be sent against an enemy; the tupilak was made in secret and had to be defeated by its victim's own power or by finding its maker. Carving it was the dangerous part, and today the word names both the spirit and the grotesque figurines that have become Greenlandic art.
source: Greenlandic oral tradition and ethnographic records

name: Harpoon
material: Wood shaft with toggle-head of bone or ivory
powers: Strikes the seal and holds it even as the line plays out.
description: The throwing weapon of the Inuit, its detachable toggle-head burying in the seal's hide and turning beneath the skin so the animal cannot pull free as the hunter hauls on the line. The design was perfected over millennia of open-water hunting and copied by the explorers who followed. Harpoons with carefully weighted heads remain among the finest tools of the Arctic.
source: Inuit oral tradition and Arctic ethnographic records

name: Ade (Yoruba Beaded Crown)
material: Glass beads, velvet or cotton cloth, seed beads
description: The ade is the beaded crown of Yoruba obas, a cone- or basket-shaped headdress whose beaded fringe veils the wearer's face. Its patterns include birds, the Ogboni-eye emblem, and the divine king's face, tying the ruler to Oduduwa and the orisa. Coronation tradition holds the veil protects subjects from the king's overwhelming gaze.
source: Yoruba coronation tradition; museum collections (British Museum, Musée du quai Branly)

name: Oshe Shango Dance Wand
powers: Said to channel Shango's lightning and to summon or cool his wrath in dance.
description: The oshe is a carved wooden dance wand of the Yoruba, crowned by a double-bladed axe, the emblem of Shango, god of thunder. Dancers of the Shango cult swing paired oshe during worship, and the blades are said to embody the deity's destructive lightning strike and regenerative force. Older examples bear carved faces of the deity or his priestesses.
source: Yoruba Shango cult tradition; museum examples

name: Opon Ifa Divination Board
description: The opon ifa is the circular wooden divination tray of Yoruba Ifa priests (babalawo), dusted with wood powder on which the client's sign is traced. The babalawo casts palm nuts or a divination chain and reads the emerging patterns under Orunmila's guidance. Tray rims are carved with Eshu's face and proverb scenes, and the board is kept from profane use.
source: Ifa divination tradition; oral knowledge of the babalawo

name: Ikenga Shrine Figure
powers: Embodies the owner's personal achievement, strength, and right hand.
description: The ikenga is a carved wooden shrine figure of Igbo men, with a seated human body, curving horns, and a sword or club in each hand. It stands for personal achievement, physical strength, and the right hand of the owner, and is kept on the family altar where offerings accompany prayers for success. The horns recall the ram and the aggressive power of the ancestor-hero.

name: Gelede Mask
description: Gelede masks are carved wooden headdresses of the Yoruba, worn tilted on the head by masqueraders who dance in honour of mothers and 'our mothers' (awon iya wa), the powerful spiritual women of the night. Each mask's crest depicts animals, scenes, or people, and the performance praises female power and works for social harmony. Practised in southern Nigeria and neighbouring Benin and Togo.
source: Yoruba oral tradition; UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage listing of Gelede

name: Edan Ogboni Staff
era: Traditional, still used in society rites
powers: Held to enforce truth and justice, sealing oaths made before the earth's authority.
description: The edan are paired brass or iron staffs of the Yoruba Ogboni (Osugbo) society, each topped by a seated human figure joined by a chain. The male-female pair stands for the moral unity of the earth and is kept on the society's altar, where oaths were sworn over it. It symbolises truth, justice, and the moral authority of the elders of the earth.
source: Ogboni society tradition; British Museum collections

name: Benin Bronze Plaque
maker: Igbesanmwan guild casters of the Igun quarter
description: Cast-brass wall plaques of the Edo Kingdom of Benin (in present-day Nigeria) once covered the Oba's palace pillars, depicting the king, warriors, and courtiers in high relief. Made by guild casters using lost-wax casting, they record royal history, protocol, and the kingdom's contact with Europeans. Taken to Europe in 1897, they remain central to restitution debate.
source: British Museum collections; Edo court history and restitution scholarship

name: The Golden Stool (Sika Dwa)
powers: Holds the soul (sunsum) of the Asante nation; its wellbeing is the nation's wellbeing.
description: The Sika Dwa, or Golden Stool, is the sacred stool of the Asante, a gold-covered stool kept unseated-on as the soul (sunsum) of the nation. Tradition holds that Okomfo Anokye called it down from heaven in the 1700s, settling it onto the lap of Osei Tutu. It may not touch the ground and remains the supreme emblem of Asante sovereignty.
source: Asante oral tradition; Manhyia Palace Museum

name: Akan Goldweight (Abrammuo)
description: Akan brass goldweights (abrammuo) are small cast-metal pieces used from the 15th century to weigh gold dust in Ghanaian trade. Figurative weights depict proverbs, animals, people, and everyday scenes, each one 'speaking' a proverb when shown to a companion. They join commerce, sculpture, and orature into a single object of Akan social life.
source: Akan trade tradition; museum collections (British Museum)

name: Kente Cloth
description: Kente is the strip-woven silk-and-cotton cloth of the Asante and Ewe, assembled from narrow bands into bold geometric patterns, each with a name and proverb meaning. Weaving was a male craft tied to the royal court; colours and motifs encode rank, occasion, and moral teaching. Asante origin tradition credits the spider Anansi with inspiring the first cloth.

name: Adinkra Cloth
material: Cotton, carved calabash stamps, tree-bark dye
description: Adinkra is a printed cotton cloth of the Akan, dyed and stamped with symbolic motifs such as the 'sankofa' bird, each carrying a proverb or moral meaning. Traditionally worn at funerals, it was stamped from carved calabash blocks with a dye made from tree bark. The symbols themselves are treated as repositories of ancestral wisdom.

name: Fon Asen Altar Staff
description: Asen are commemorative altar staffs of the Fon of Benin (Dahomey), forged iron poles topped by figurative scenes - ancestor portraits, animals, or scenes of daily life - set in clay or iron bases. Placed by the ancestor altar of the compound, they receive offerings during family rites and keep the dead present in Vodun practice.
source: Fon ancestor ritual; museum collections (Musée du quai Branly)

name: Zangbeto Masquerade Costume
description: The zangbeto is a towering cone-shaped costume of plaited straw or raffia worn by the masked guardians of the night in Fon towns of Benin. Hidden inside, the performer makes the tall figure appear to spin and dance of its own accord, embodying the zangbeto spirit that patrols against witches, thieves, and wrongdoers.

name: Dahomey Applique Cloth
description: Dahomey (Fon) applique cloths are rectangular textiles on which cut-out cloth figures are sewn to tell royal history and proverbs. Commissioned for the Fon court, they depict kings, warriors, and the kingdom's celebrated women soldiers, and were also carried as banners and umbrella covers in royal processions.
source: Fon court tradition; museum collections (Musée du quai Branly)

name: Dogon Kanaga Mask
description: The kanaga is a wooden headdress of the Dogon of Mali with a vertical crest and crossed bars, danced by masked societies at dama funerals and the great Sigi ceremonies. The crossed arms echo Amma's creation and the structure of the world, while the mask mediates between the living and the spirits of the dead.
source: Dogon masked society tradition; ethnographic studies (Griaule school)

name: Chiwara Headdress
description: The chiwara is a carved wooden headdress of the Bamana (Bambara) of Mali, shaped like an antelope with a long neck and horns. It is worn in pairs during field dances that honour the mythical chiwara who taught humanity agriculture. The vertical zigzag crest and pierced back recall the sun's rays and the roan antelope.

name: Bogolanfini Mud Cloth
description: Bogolanfini, or mud cloth, is a Bamana textile of Mali painted with fermented river-mud dye over a yellow ground to create dark geometric patterns. Made by women, the cloth records proverbs and historical knowledge and was worn at initiations and by hunters; its designs are held to protect and to transmit clan memory.

name: Sabar Drum
description: The sabar is the lead drum of Wolof and Serer music of Senegal, a single-headed drum played with one hand and a curved stick. Played at ceremonies and wrestling matches, its rhythms are named and can 'talk', and master drummers lead communal dance. Sabar ensembles anchor celebration and social life across Senegal.

name: Xalam Lute
material: Wood, skin, gut or nylon strings
description: The xalam is a plucked five-string lute of the Wolof of Senegal, with a wooden bowl body and skin head, played by griots to accompany praise-songs and narratives. Two melody and three rhythm strings let one musician produce interlocking lines, and the instrument is central to West African praise orature.

name: Dan Mask
description: Dan masks of the Ivory Coast are carved wooden face masks with narrow eye slits and a smooth, reflective surface, worn at entertainment, justice, and initiation. A mask's power lies in the spirit (gle) it embodies; each is owned by a community or family and handled with ritual care, oiled and fed to keep its force alive.

name: Baule Goli Mask
description: The goli is a round-faced, carved mask of the Baule people of the Ivory Coast, painted and worn at village dances and funerals. Goli performances follow a fixed sequence of mask types that mirror the cosmos and communal order, and the mask is associated with the goli spirit forces that lend the dance its authority.

name: Tuareg Takuba Sword
description: The takuba is the straight-bladed, cross-hilted sword of the Tuareg of the Sahel, carried by warriors and today worn as a mark of honour. Forged iron blades are paired with decorated leather scabbards, often dyed and embossed. The takuba historically signalled the status of its bearer and featured in Tuareg duels and raids.

name: Agadez Cross Pendant
powers: Worn as a protective amulet, with the arms said to guard the wearer in life's directions.
description: The Agadez cross, or tanaghilt, is a silver pendant of the Tuareg made in Agadez, Niger, with a distinctive cruciform design of four or more arms. Crosses are given to mark passages through life, cast by the city's smiths (inadan), and worn as protective amulets; each regional cross carries its own name and meaning.

name: Sao Bronze Bracelet
description: Bronze and copper ornaments cast by the Sao people of the Lake Chad basin, an urban civilisation that flourished in what is now Chad for over a millennium. Excavated bracelets, anklets, and figurines from Sao mound sites show accomplished lost-wax casting; major finds are kept at the National Museum of N'Djamena and studied as key evidence of ancient Central African metalwork.
source: Sao archaeological finds; National Museum of N'Djamena

name: Bamum Beaded Throne (Mandu Yenu)
description: The Mandu Yenu is the beaded royal throne of the Bamum kingdom of Cameroon, a low platform completely covered with glass beads in layered patterns of royal symbolism. The 19th-century throne of King Nsangu is among the finest, framing the seated king with beaded figures and the two-faced mask of royal justice. Beaded thrones proclaimed the divine rank of the fon.
source: British Museum collections (Mandu Yenu of King Nsangu)

name: Bamileke Elephant Mask
era: Traditional, still used in chiefdom rites
description: Beaded wooden masks of the Bamileke of the Cameroon Grassfields, often shaped as an elephant head with rounded ears and trunk, are worn by the society that enforces chiefly authority. The elephant mask links the wearer to the fon's power and the forest, and beadwork in royal colours marks noble membership. Attribution to specific chiefdoms varies across museum collections.
source: Museum collections of Cameroon Grassfields royal arts

name: Nkul Slit Gong
description: The nkul is a wooden slit gong of the Cameroon forests, a hollowed log with a longitudinal slit, beaten with a stick to send messages across valleys and to accompany ritual. Different strokes mimic the tones of speech, and nkul signals have historically announced news, danger, and ceremonial gatherings to whole villages.

name: Nkisi Nkondi Power Figure
material: Carved wood, iron blades and nails, mirror, pigment
powers: Held to hunt wrongdoers, seal oaths, and settle disputes; each driven blade records a sworn act.
description: An nkisi nkondi is a Kongo power figure of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, a carved wooden figure into which nails, blades, and other matter were driven to activate or seal its power. The nganga (ritual specialist) activated it to hunt wrongdoers, enforce oaths, and settle disputes; the embedded blades record each act sworn before it.
source: Kongo ritual tradition; museum collections (British Museum, Brooklyn Museum)

name: Lukasa Memory Board
description: The lukasa is a wooden memory board of the Luba of the DRC, its surface studded with beads and pins arranged to encode history, genealogy, and royal protocol. A court historian (mumbudye) 'reads' the board by touch as a mnemonic for sacred knowledge. The arrangement of each board varies with its owner and the legends it preserves.
source: Luba court tradition; scholarly studies (M. Nooter Roberts)

name: Kuba Beaded Cup
material: Wood, glass beads, cowrie shells, brass studs
description: Ceremonial drinking cups of the Kuba kingdom of the DRC, carved from wood and densely covered with cowrie shells, brass studs, and glass beads in geometric patterns. Owned by Kuba kings and nobles, they were used in court ceremony and kept in the palace treasury; some cups take human or animal form.

name: Kuba Ndop Royal Figure
description: The ndop is a carved wooden portrait figure of a Kuba king of the DRC, seated cross-legged with the king's personal emblem (ibol) carved beside him. Each ndop commemorated a ruler's reign and was kept in a sacred house of the palace; the figure's gesture and pattern of scarification identify the individual king.
source: Kuba royal tradition; museum collections (British Museum)

name: Teke Kidumu Mask
description: Teke 'kidumu' masks of the Republic of the Congo are flat, round wooden face masks decorated with painted geometric designs in red, white, and black. Worn by men of the kidumu society at initiations and funerals, the mask's patterns are said to allude to the Teke origin story of a great turtle from whose back the world grew.

name: Chokwe Pwo Mask
material: Carved wood, pigment, fibre and feathers
description: The pwo is the carved female mask of the Chokwe of Angola, with a finely finished face, scarification marks, and a headdress of fibre and feathers. Danced at initiations and celebrations, it honours the idealised ancestress; its calm, polished beauty marks the grace expected of Chokwe women.

name: Chokwe Chief's Throne
description: Carved wooden chief's thrones of the Chokwe of Angola, with a seat supported by figures of ancestors, chiefs, and scenes of everyday life, often studded with brass tacks. The throne proclaims the dignity of the soba and the continuity of the chieftaincy; the supporting figures were personal emblems of the ruler.

name: Maasai Nborr Collar
description: The nborr is a flat, beaded collar of the Maasai of Kenya, built on a leather or wire base and covered with glass-bead patterns in red, white, blue, and black. Worn by women at ceremonies and by young men (moran), the collars signal age-set, status, and clan, and beaded colours carry agreed social meanings.

name: Maasai Rungu Club
description: The rungu is a short wooden throwing club of the Maasai of Kenya, with a knobbed head and tapering handle, carried by herders and moran. Traditionally used to guard cattle against predators and in ceremony, the rungu today is a symbol of authority, often ornamented and carried by elders at gatherings.

name: Maasai Shuka Cloth
era: Contemporary, evolving from traditional hide cloth
description: The shuka is the checked, blanket-like cloth worn wrapped around the body by Maasai of Kenya and Tanzania, traditionally dyed in red tones. Red is said to honour Maasai cattle culture and the warrior ideal; the cloth's patterns vary by community, and modern production blends factory cotton with older styles of hide and woven dress.

name: Ngoma Drum (Swahili Coast)
description: Ngoma drums of the Swahili coast of Tanzania are wooden drums, often barrel- or goblet-shaped, played at weddings, dances, and ritual. 'Ngoma' names drum, dance, and festivity together; coastal ensembles with distinct drum parts accompanied celebration and were also used in spirit ceremonies to summon the pepo.

name: Makonde Shetani Figure
description: Makonde 'shetani' carvings of Tanzania are dark hardwood figures of contorted, expressive spirits, made by Makonde carvers from the 1950s onward. They depict shetani - capricious ancestral and bush spirits - in twisted poses that blur human and animal form, and are celebrated in Swahili and international art as a meditation on the spirit world.

name: Zanzibar Dhow
description: The dhow (jahazi) of Zanzibar is a lateen-sailed wooden vessel built on the Swahili coast for fishing, cargo, and the monsoon trade. Dhow hulls were traditionally sewn with coconut coir and caulked, and the vessels carried ivory, cloves, and mangrove poles across the Indian Ocean, tying the coast's seafaring to its maritime spirit lore.

name: Buganda Royal Drum (Mujaguzo)
description: The mujaguzo are the royal drums of the Buganda kingdom of Uganda, a set of tuned drums beaten at coronations, the accession of chiefs, and war. The principal drum, also called Mujaguzo, is kept in the palace and beaten only on state occasions; the drums were regarded as the voice of the kabaka and his ancestors.

name: Baganda Barkcloth (Olubugo)
material: Beaten inner bark of the mutuba fig tree
description: Olubugo is the barkcloth of the Baganda of Uganda, made by beating the inner bark of the mutuba (fig) tree into a soft, chestnut-brown textile. Men traditionally prepared the cloth, which was worn by kings and chiefs, used in burials, and remains a sacred material; UNESCO lists Baganda barkcloth-making as intangible cultural heritage.
source: Ganda barkcloth tradition; UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage

name: Ethiopian Processional Cross
description: Ethiopian processional crosses are tall brass or silver crosses with a lattice of openwork tracery, carried on a staff before the clergy in Ethiopian Orthodox liturgy. Each cross is unique, and their intricate patterns symbolise the Tree of Life and the victory of Christ; the cross is held to carry divine protection over the faithful.

name: Jebena Coffee Pot
description: The jebena is the round, clay coffee pot of Ethiopia with a long neck and a pouring spout, used in the elaborate Ethiopian coffee ceremony. Coffee beans are roasted, ground, and brewed three rounds in the jebena, and the pot sits at the centre of hospitality and social life, symbolising friendship and community.

name: Ethiopian Ketab Protective Scroll
material: Parchment, ink, leather or cloth cover
powers: Worn or hung to ward off evil spirits, illness, and the harm attributed to buda.
description: Ketab are protective prayer scrolls of the Ethiopian Orthodox tradition, parchment strips inscribed with prayers, names, and devotional images, rolled and worn or hung as amulets. Written by debtera (church scholars) and diviners, they guard against evil spirits, illness, and the harm believed to come from buda. Their style ranges from simple folded slips to elaborate illustrated rolls.
source: Ethiopian magical scroll tradition; scholarly studies (J. Mercier)

name: Kalinga Royal Drum
description: The Kalinga is the most sacred of the royal drums of Rwanda, a decorated drum of the mwami's court that was beaten only at the most solemn ceremonies of kingship. Along with the court's other drums it accompanied the dances and rituals that affirmed the king's divine authority; after the monarchy fell, the original is said to be preserved abroad or in the national collection.

name: Somali Dabqaad Incense Burner
description: The dabqaad is a clay or soapstone incense burner of Somalia, its bowl raised on short legs and covered by a perforated lid from which smoke rises. Frankincense and myrrh smoulder in it at home to perfume rooms and welcome guests, keeping alive the incense tradition of the Horn of Africa.

name: Mahafaly Aloalo Funerary Post
description: The aloalo are tall carved funerary posts of the Mahafaly people of southwestern Madagascar, erected on family tombs and topped with figures of people, birds (often the cattle egret), and cattle. Their scenes honour the life and wealth of the deceased and the ancestors, and they stand as public memorials bound to the island's ancestral rites.

name: Zulu Iziqu Necklace
material: Carved wood or bone blocks, fibre
description: The iziqu is the beaded or block necklace of a Zulu warrior, made of carved wooden or bone blocks strung on fibre and worn across the chest as a record of valour. Each block is said to represent an enemy killed or a brave deed, so the necklace was a personal chronicle of a man's martial history, worn at dances and ceremonies.

name: Zulu Iwisa Knobkerrie
description: The iwisa (knobkerrie) is a Zulu club with a heavy round knob and a straight handle, carried by warriors and later by chiefs and officials as a staff of rank. It was both a close-combat weapon and, in peace, a badge of authority; elaborately carved examples were made for chiefs and are still carried at ceremonies.

name: Zulu Ukhamba Beer Pot
description: The ukhamba is the fired clay beer pot of the Zulu, a round, low-necked vessel used to brew and serve utshwala, the sorghum beer central to ceremony and hospitality. Beer brewed in the ukhamba is shared at marriages, funerals, and community gatherings, and a well-made pot is prized for its strength and fine finish.

name: Xhosa Beadwork
description: Xhosa beadwork of South Africa uses imported glass beads on leather or cotton to make necklaces, aprons, and headdresses worn at initiation and marriage. Colour combinations carry coded messages of love, status, and lineage, and the beaded garments of Xhosa initiates mark the passage from boyhood to manhood in the circumcision school.

name: Mbira Dzavadzimu
description: The mbira dzavadzimu is the lamellophone of the Shona of Zimbabwe, a wooden board with metal keys mounted over a gourd resonator that buzzes with a shell or bottle-top. Played to summon the ancestors (vadzimu) at ceremonies, its interlocking patterns accompany singing and call the spirits to guide the community.

name: Soapstone Bird of Great Zimbabwe
description: The soapstone birds of Great Zimbabwe are carved stone birds, about 40 cm tall, with human lips and outstretched wings, set atop monoliths in the ancient city. They are believed to have been royal emblems of the Shona state that ruled the stone city, and the bird was later adopted as the national symbol of Zimbabwe.
source: Archaeological finds at Great Zimbabwe; UNESCO World Heritage

name: Chipendani Mouth Bow
description: The chipendani is a small mouth-bow of the Shona of Zimbabwe, a curved wooden bow with a fibre string, played by plucking while the mouth shapes the tone. It is a personal instrument of young herders, and its light, rhythmic notes accompany the passing of time and courtship in rural life.

name: Lozi Royal Barge
description: The Lozi royal barge (nalikwanda) is the great wooden vessel that carries the Litunga of the Lozi people of Zambia across the flooded Zambezi at the Kuomboka ceremony. Covered with an immense shroud and propelled by dozens of paddlers, the barge marks the king's seasonal move from lowland to highland palace, a pageant of kingship and river lore.

name: Gule Wamkulu Mask
description: The gule wamkulu masks of the Chewa of Malawi are carved wooden face masks worn at the Nyau dance of the gule wamkulu society, performed at initiations, funerals, and memorials. The masked dancers embody ancestral spirits and animals, and the Nyau tradition, listed by UNESCO, is a key keeper of Chewa history and law.
source: Chewa Nyau tradition; UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage

name: Makonde Lipiko Mask
description: Lipiko masks of the Makonde of Mozambique are wooden face masks with protruding lips and painted detail, worn by initiates in the mapiko dance that closes initiation rites. The performers are said to embody spirits of the dead and ancestors, and the masks are kept hidden from the uninitiated.

name: Tagine Cooking Vessel
description: The tagine is the conical clay cooking vessel of Morocco, whose tall lid traps steam so that slow-braised stews cook in very little water. The same word names the dish it cooks; the pot is glazed, set over a brazier or stove, and has become emblematic of Moroccan cooking and hospitality across North Africa.

name: Burnous Cloak
description: The burnous is the hooded, sleeveless woollen cloak of the Berbers of North Africa, woven in one piece with a pointed hood (qob). Worn by men over other garments, it shields against sun and cold and marks status; finely embroidered burnouses are reserved for ceremonies and celebrations.

name: Tizerzai Brooch
powers: Fastens the dress and is worn for protection, with engraved motifs said to avert harm.
description: The tizerzai is a large silver brooch of the Amazigh women of Morocco, a crescent- or triangle-shaped clasp used to fasten the shoulder of the dress, fitted with a long pin and decorative chainwork. It is both a practical garment fastener and a piece of protective jewellery, often engraved and embellished with coral or enamel.

name: Kabyle Earthenware
description: Kabyle earthenware of Algeria is burnished, hand-built clay pottery made by Kabyle women in the Djurdjura mountains, shaped without a wheel and decorated with painted or incised geometric motifs. Cooking pots, water jars, and grain bowls served daily life; the reddish clay pieces are famed for their clean lines and remain a living craft of the Berber home.

name: Chaoui Aures Kilim
description: Chaoui (Aures) weavings of Algeria are wool carpets and blankets woven on ground looms by Amazigh women of the Aures mountains, with bold stripes and geometric medallions in red, brown, and cream. Woven for the home and for dowries, the textiles carry regional motifs whose meanings are handed down in the weaving tradition.
source: Studies of Amazigh weaving (e.g. Ianthe Reswick)

name: Tunisian Chechia Cap
description: The chechia is the brimless, red felt cap of Tunisia, traditionally made by hand-felting wool and dyeing it crimson, then shaping it over a wooden mould. Worn by men across the Maghreb as a mark of Tunisian identity, it was produced in the chechia craft quarter of Tunis and given as a gift of distinction.

name: Gourgui Water Jar
description: The gourgui is a porous clay water jar of Tunisia, kept in the cool shade of the home so that evaporation chills the water inside. Its narrow neck and globular body recall ancient amphorae; similar jars across the Maghreb were central to daily water storage and hospitality.

name: Garamantian Rock-Art Chariot
description: Rock-art depictions of horses and chariots carved in the Tadrart Acacus and Messak mountains of the Fezzan, Libya, are linked in scholarship to the Garamantes, the Saharan power whose chariot-based trade crossed the desert. The engravings, several thousand years old, show lightweight chariots in motion and form a major record of Saharan history.
source: UNESCO rock-art sites of Tadrart Acacus; Garamantian archaeology

name: Canopic Jar
era: Ancient Egyptian (Old Kingdom to Ptolemaic era)
description: Canopic jars are the lidded stone or pottery vessels of ancient Egypt that held the embalmed organs of the dead, each guarded by one of the Four Sons of Horus. Made from the Old Kingdom onward, they were buried with the mummy so the body would be whole in the afterlife; Anubis, god of mummification, presides over the rite.
source: Ancient Egyptian funerary archaeology; museum collections

name: Ancient Egyptian Kohl Tube
description: Ancient Egyptian kohl tubes are slender cosmetic containers, often of wood, stone, or faience, used to hold kohl eye-paint. Applied with a stick, kohl protected the eyes from sun and flies and carried religious meaning, its dark-lined eye echoing the apotropaic gaze of Horus; fine decorated examples survive from the New Kingdom.
source: Museum collections (British Museum, Metropolitan Museum of Art)

name: Sudanese Kaskara Sword
description: The kaskara is a straight, double-edged sword with a plain iron cross-guard and disc pommel, carried in Sudan and adjacent regions into the 20th century. It descends from medieval Arab forms and served as a fighting blade and ceremonial weapon; many bear inscriptions, marks, or leather-wrapped grips, and were worn as signs of honour.

name: Sudanese Girba Water-Skin
description: The girba is a water vessel of Sudan made from a whole tanned animal hide, treated to be watertight, with openings at the neck and legs. Carried by travellers and herders across the Sahel and Nubia, it keeps water cool through evaporation; its shape and use are documented in travel accounts of the Nile lands.
source: Travel accounts of the Nile lands; museum collections

name: Vajra of Indra
description: Double-ended thunderbolt of Indra, king of the devas, said in the Puranas to have been forged from the bones of the sage Dadhichi after he gave up his life for the gods. In the Rigveda Indra wields the vajra to slay Vritra the drought serpent, and the weapon endures in Hindu and Buddhist iconography as a marker of kingship over storms and victory.
maker: crafted in myth by the god Tvashtar

name: Trishula of Shiva
description: Three-pronged spear sacred to Shiva, the destroyer, whose prongs stand for creation, preservation and destruction, or for the three gunas that compose the world. Shiva carries the trishula in Puranic sculpture and story, and devotees plant iron trishulas at cremation grounds and shrine thresholds, where the weapon is said to pierce ignorance and drive away evil spirits.
source: Shiva Purana and Shaiva iconographic tradition

name: Sudarshana Chakra
description: Whirling discus carried by Vishnu, the Sudarshana Chakra, described in the Puranas as a blazing thousand-spoked weapon that flies to its target and returns to its master. It appears in Vishnu's upper right hand beside the conch, lotus and mace, and is hurled in avatar legends, such as the slaying of the demons Jay and Vijay, against foes who cannot be defeated by other means.

name: Shiva Lingam
description: Aniconic emblem of Shiva worshipped as a polished stone or carved shaft rising from a yoni base, standing for the god's infinite and formless power. Lingams are anointed daily with water, milk and bilva leaves across India, and the Puranas hold that Shiva once appeared as a column of fire whose ends neither Brahma nor Vishnu could find, a legend re-enacted in the lingam's worship.

name: Rudraksha Mala
description: Rosary of dried rudraksha seeds, each furrowed bead sacred to Shiva, strung as a meditation mala worn by ascetics and devotees. Hindu tradition holds that the rudraksha tree sprang from Shiva's tears, that beads with five natural grooves are most auspicious, and that chanting while turning the mala purifies the mind and body and grants steadiness to the devotee.
source: Shaiva devotional tradition and Puranic legend of Shiva's tears

name: Ganesh Idol
description: Clay or metal image of the elephant-headed god Ganesha, remover of obstacles, set at thresholds, workplaces and festival altars across India. At Ganesh Chaturthi, clay idols are installed, prayed over and immersed in rivers, re-enacting the myth of the boy whose head was replaced by an elephant's after Shiva beheaded him, as told in the Ganesha Purana and local stories.
source: Ganesha Purana; Ganesh Chaturthi festival practice

name: Diya Oil Lamp
description: Small clay or brass lamp whose cotton wick burns in ghee or oil, lit at dusk in Hindu homes and temples for worship. During Diwali, rows of diyas are set out to welcome the goddess Lakshmi and drive back the dark, and the lamp's steady flame is read as a sign of auspiciousness and of the triumph of light over shadow in the festival's folklore.

name: Mangal Kalasha
description: Copper or clay pot filled with water and topped with a coconut and mango leaves, set on a bed of rice to open Hindu ceremonies. The kalasha is treated as a vessel of the divine, inviting a presiding deity to dwell in its water, and it is carried before brides, raised at temple consecrations and used in house blessings as a source of prosperity and good fortune.
source: Hindu ritual manuals (grihya sutra tradition) and festival practice

name: Puja Thali
description: Brass tray that carries the elements of Hindu worship, such as kumkum powder, turmeric, rice, flowers, incense and a burning camphor flame, as it is waved before a deity or an honoured guest. In households the thali is circulated so onlookers can receive the darshan of the flame, and the arrangement of its offerings follows the ritual order of the puja.

name: Brass Urli
description: Wide shallow brass bowl of South Indian households, filled with water and floating flowers or marigold blossoms and set in entrance courts and courtyards as a marker of hospitality and blessing. Urlis are also used as ritual lamps when oil-lit wicks are floated on the water, a practice seen at weddings and festival doorways across Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
source: South Indian household and wedding practice

name: Tandoor
description: Cylindrical clay oven sunk into the earth or a hearth, fired from below so breads and meats cook against its hot walls, used across North India and the Punjab plains. In village households the tandoor is a shared daily fixture, and its flames carry a homely, auspicious aura; flatbreads are pressed by hand against the clay and baked in seconds.

name: Sankha Conch
description: Right-whorled conch shell blown at Hindu ceremonies and held by Vishnu as Panchajanya, the war-conch of the god. In the Puranas Vishnu sounds the conch before battle, and the sankha is still blown to open worship and marriage rites, its deep note believed to dispel inauspicious forces and to mark the boundary of sacred space.
source: Vishnu Purana; Hindu temple and marriage ritual

name: Veena
description: Ancient Indian lute of gourd and wood, the instrument of Saraswati, goddess of learning and the arts, who holds it in her hands as she sits upon her lotus. Played in Carnatic and Hindustani music, the veena is treated as the archetype of melody, and Saraswati's veena is said in the tradition to sound the knowledge of the world itself.
maker: luthiers of Tanjore and the Deccan
source: Natya Shastra and Puranic iconography of Saraswati

name: Tabla
description: Pair of small hand drums, the larger metal-bodied bayan and the smaller wooden dayan, tuned together and played with fingers and palms, central to Hindustani classical rhythm. Tabla playing is learned through rhythmic syllables such as dha, tin and na, and the instrument anchors devotional song and dance, carrying the beat of both court music and folk performance.
maker: tabla makers of Delhi and Banaras
source: Hindustani musicological tradition and instrument history

name: Tulwar
description: Curved single-edged sword of the Indian subcontinent, a cavalry blade with a distinctive hilt whose disc pommel and crossguard appear in tales of Rajput and Mughal warriors. The tulwar was carried as both weapon and emblem of rank, and folk tales of battles, honour and oath-taking treat the sword as a binding object passed down as an heirloom of warrior families.
source: Arms museum collections and court chronicles

name: Katar
culture: Deccan and South Indian martial culture
description: Push dagger of South India and the Deccan, held by its H-shaped grip and driven with a punch rather than a cut, a weapon of close-quarter combat and ceremonial display. Katars appear in sculpted panels of royal processions and temple walls, and the dagger's distinctive handle makes it an instantly recognised emblem of Indian arms in courtly art and museum collections.
source: Arms museum collections and temple sculpture

name: Khanda
description: Double-edged straight sword of the Sikh tradition, emblem of the Khalsa and of Sikh martial piety. The khanda also names the double-edged emblem that crowns the Sikh nishan sahib banner, and Sikh tradition holds the sword as a symbol of justice, truth and the duty to defend the defenceless, carried and honoured in Sikh religious life.
source: Sikh religious tradition and panthic practice

name: Kirpan
description: Curved sword or dagger that every initiated Sikh carries as one of the five articles of faith, a physical pledge to uphold justice and protect the vulnerable. Forged of steel and worn at the waist or in a shoulder strap, the kirpan is at once a religious obligation and a reminder of the warrior-saint ideal of Sikhism, never used without cause.

name: Kada Bangle
description: Steel bangle worn by Sikhs on the right wrist as one of the five articles of the Khalsa, a ring with no beginning or end that stands for the unbroken bond with the divine. Sikh tradition requires the kada to be worn with commitment to the Guru's path, and it is treated as a visible sign of faith, humility and belonging to the community.

name: Mangalsutra
description: Necklace of black beads and gold, or a gold pendant on a cord, tied by the groom around the bride's neck during the Hindu wedding rite. The mangalsutra is worn for the rest of the married woman's life and is read in folklore as a powerful talisman of her husband's life and of the marriage bond, never to be removed or broken.
source: Hindu wedding ritual and marriage custom

name: Banarasi Sari
description: Handwoven silk sari of Varanasi, made with gold and silver zari thread in patterns of mangoes, flowers and mehrab arches that have been prized in Indian bridal wear for centuries. Weavers of the city have produced banarasi brocades since Mughal times, and the sari is treated as a family heirloom passed between generations of brides.

name: Phulkari
description: Punjabi shawl or dupatta embroidered on the reverse side with silk thread so that rough, bright flower motifs bloom on the front, worked by women for weddings and festivals. A phulkari is part of a bride's trousseau, and its stitches carry the love and skill of the women who made it over months, each pattern named for the flowers and shapes it shows.

name: Pashmina Shawl
description: Fine shawl woven from the under-fleece of Himalayan pashmina goats, spun and woven by Kashmiri artisans into a fabric so soft it is said to pass through a finger ring. Pashmina weaving of the Kashmir valley is famed worldwide, and the shawl is treasured as a winter garment and a symbol of the region's long craft tradition.
source: Craft history of the Kashmir valley

name: Sacred Tooth Relic
description: Relic of a tooth of the Buddha enshrined in the Temple of the Sacred Tooth in Kandy, the most venerated Buddhist object in Sri Lanka. According to the Mahavamsa the tooth was smuggled to the island from India and carried by successive rulers, and annual perahera processions honour it as guardian of the land and of its kings.
era: according to tradition, 4th century AD onwards
maker: enshrined by Sinhalese kings; reliquaries by court goldsmiths
source: Mahavamsa and the chronicle of the Tooth Relic (Dalada-vamsa)

name: Kandyan Crown
description: Royal crown of the Kandyan kingdom of central Sri Lanka, a jewel-studded, turban-like headdress that the last Kandyan king, Sri Vikrama Rajasinha, surrendered to the British in 1815. The crown and the rest of the Kandyan regalia are held today in museum collections and stand for the sovereignty of the highland kingdom and its court rituals.
source: Museum holdings and Kandyan court records (British Museum collections)

name: Kastane Sword
description: Sinhalese ceremonial sword with an elaborately carved handle, often a lion or demon head in ivory, worn at the waist for court dress and ritual. In Kandyan and low-country rites the kastane is used to invoke and control demonic spirits, and it appears in the exorcism traditions connected with the demon lineages of Sri Lanka, where the sword's presence is believed to command the unseen.
source: Museum collections and ritual ethnography (J Intangible Cultural Heritage)

name: Alms Bowl Relic
description: The alms bowl of the Buddha, said in Buddhist tradition to have been brought to Sri Lanka and venerated as a relic after his parinirvana. The Mahavamsa records the bowl being kept and honoured at a shrine, though no such relic is verifiably present today, and the story survives as an article of faith rather than as proven history.

name: Gata Bera Drum
description: Large cylindrical drum of Sri Lanka, slung at the hip and beaten with sticks or hands at festivals, temple rites and healing ceremonies. The gata bera's rhythms summon blessings in Buddhist perahera processions and drive the masked exorcism dances that pacify the disease demons of the Sinhalese tradition.

name: Sanni Yaksha Mask
description: Carved wooden mask of a Sinhalese disease demon, one of the eighteen sanni masks painted in vivid colours and worn in exorcism ceremonies. Each mask portrays a specific affliction such as fever, madness or jaundice, and the dance of the mask is performed to trick the demon and dismiss it from the sick body, a practice known as tovil.
source: Sinhalese ritual ethnography and mask-carving tradition

name: Ajrak
description: Block-printed shawl of Sindh, stamped in dark indigo and crimson with geometric border patterns, worn across the shoulder and used to cover sacred objects. Ajrak printing is a hereditary craft of Sindhi towns, and the shawl is a marker of Sindhi identity, draped at weddings, offered to guests and presented as a mark of honour.
source: Craft history of Sindh and Sindhi cultural practice

name: Sindhi Topi
description: Embroidered cylindrical cap of Sindh, worn by men and at festivals, with a band of stitched mirror-work and a rounded crown. The sindhi topi is a national symbol of the province, worn with the ajrak shawl, and Sindhi folklore holds that the cap carries the honour and pride of the wearer, so that to knock it off is a grave insult.

name: Butterfly Jigha
description: Jewel-studded turban ornament of Mughal court fashion, shaped as a butterfly with a spring that quivers as the wearer moves, pinned to the turban by nobles and princes. Mughal miniature painting shows such jigha ornaments at court, and surviving examples in museum collections are worked in gold with gemstones, worn in the regions that became Pakistan.
source: Museum holdings (e.g. V&A O73036) and Mughal painting

name: Naqqara Drum
description: Pair of kettledrums struck with sticks, carried before rulers and beaten at Sufi shrines and processions across Pakistan and the wider Muslim world. In the Punjab and Sindh the naqqara announces royal arrivals and festival days, and its deep paired notes are said to carry the blessing of the occasion through the crowd.
maker: drum makers of the Punjab and Sindh
source: Indo-Islamic court and shrine musical tradition

name: Karahi
description: Deep rounded wok of cast iron or steel used across Pakistan to cook the spiced curry that shares its name, set over an open flame. In homes and bazaars the karahi is the daily vessel of celebratory and communal cooking, and its name has passed from the pan itself to a whole style of Pakistani dish served hot from the pan.

name: Rilli Quilt
description: Patchwork quilt of Sindh, sewn by women from recycled cotton in geometric bands of triangles and diamonds, kept for winter bedding and given at weddings. Rilli-making is passed between mothers and daughters, and the quilt's bright patterns are read as a record of the maker's skill and the household's fortunes.

name: Khukuri
description: Curved blade of the Gurkha warrior tradition, broadest near the tip, used for cutting, chopping and ceremony in Nepal. The khukuri is carried in its leather scabbard with two small companion knives, and Nepali folk belief holds that once drawn the blade should taste blood before it is sheathed again, a custom linked to its history as a war weapon.
source: Nepali folk custom and Gurkha regimental tradition

name: Mukut Crown
description: Jewel-set crown of the Malla and Shah kings of Nepal, worn at state and religious ceremonies and linked to the goddess Taleju, protector of the royal dynasties. The Newar tradition of the living goddess Kumari also includes a crown placed on the girl deity during festivals, echoing the belief that the right to rule comes by divine favour.
source: Newar court tradition and museum regalia holdings

name: Thangka
description: Painted or embroidered scroll of Buddhist deities and mandalas, framed in silk and hung in Tibetan Buddhist monasteries and homes of the Himalayan world. Thangkas are painted with mineral pigments to exact iconographic rule, and the images are regarded as aids to meditation and carriers of the blessing of the figures they depict.
material: cotton or silk, mineral pigments, gold

name: Singing Bowl
description: Metal bowl that rings a sustained tone when its rim is rubbed with a wooden striker, used in Himalayan Buddhist ritual for offerings and meditation. The bowls are held to clear and focus the mind, and their sound is used to open and close ceremonies in the monasteries of Nepal and Tibet, where the ringing is read as an offering to the deities.
source: Himalayan ritual practice and craft tradition

name: Mani Wall
description: Long low wall of carved stones inscribed with the mantra Om Mani Padme Hum, raised beside mountain paths in the Himalayas as a prayer in stone. Travellers pass the mani wall keeping it to their right and add their own stones, so that the wall grows as a living offering along the route, and the carved stones are believed to carry blessing to all who walk by.

name: Sherpa Pangden
description: Striped front apron woven and worn by Sherpa married women over their chuba, the pangden's narrow red, white and black stripes marking the wearer's married status. The aprons are woven on backstrap looms from sheep and yak wool, and Sherpa tradition regards them as a badge of the household and of womanhood, also woven in neighbouring Tibet.
source: Sherpa weaving and dress ethnography (Dolma Sherpa)

name: Dorje
description: Ritual thunderbolt of Bhutanese and Tibetan Buddhism, a bronze sceptre with five-pronged ends that stands for the indestructible method of enlightenment. Vajra in Sanskrit, the dorje is paired with the ritual bell in monastic hand rituals and echoes the old thunder-weapon of the gods in Himalayan ritual art, where it is held by monks during ceremonies.

name: Drilbu Bell
description: Ritual hand bell of Himalayan Buddhism, struck and rung during ceremonies and paired with the dorje sceptre, cast in an alloy that rings with a long clear note. The drilbu's sound is held to summon compassion and mark the moments of a ritual, and its handle carries the face of a deity, most often Prajnaparamita, the goddess of wisdom.

name: Bhutanese Festival Mask
description: Carved and painted wooden mask worn by dancers in the cham dances of Bhutanese monasteries, taking the faces of fierce deities, animals and the skeleton guardians of the faith. The masks appear at tsechu festivals held yearly at the dzongs, where the masked dances are believed to bless onlookers and drive away evil, and where each mask's design follows strict iconographic rules.

name: Nakshi Kantha
description: Embroidered quilt of Bengal, sewn by village women from stacked layers of old saris and dhotis, stitched with running thread into scenes of flowers, birds and everyday life. A nakshi kantha made for a bride is a gift of love and skill, and the craft is named for the fine nakshi, or patterned, stitching that covers the cloth with motifs handed down between generations.

name: Dhakai Jamdani
description: Handwoven muslin of Dhaka, patterned with fine cotton motifs of floral and geometric forms woven into the cloth on the loom. Jamdani weaving is a craft of the Dhaka region practised for centuries and protected as an intangible heritage, and the sheer, patterned fabric has been prized as ceremonial dress across Bengal and beyond.
source: UNESCO intangible heritage listing and craft history

name: Ghot Pot
description: Brass or clay pot placed before the bride and groom in the ashirbad blessing of Bengali weddings, filled with paddy, durba grass and a red-and-white thread tied around its mouth. The ghot pot is a token of fertility and prosperity, and its placement during the blessing is part of the ritual good wishes spoken over the couple.
source: Bengali Hindu wedding custom (Antrocom marriage-customs study)

name: Ektara
description: One-stringed lute of rural Bengal, a gourd or bamboo body with a single steel string struck and plucked, carried by wandering Baul singers. The ektara's thin drone accompanies the mystic songs of the Bauls of Bengal, and the instrument is bound to the oral tradition of the region's wandering bards, who sing of the divine within the human body.

name: Khyber Knife
description: Straight-bladed knife of the frontier regions of Afghanistan and the Khyber, with a wide spine and simple handle, worn at the belt and used for cutting and defence. Named for the Khyber Pass, the knife is a familiar article of the Pashtun belt and appears in the material culture of the borderlands, carried for daily work and carried as a mark of the bearer.
material: steel, horn or bone handle, leather

name: Herati Carpet
description: Hand-knotted carpet of Herat in western Afghanistan, woven in wool with repeating geometric and floral medallion designs that have been exported for centuries. Herat's carpet trade flourished under the Timurid court, and the rugs are laid as prized household and prayer carpets, with patterns passed between weaving families and named for the city that produced them.
source: Carpet history of the Herat weaving region

name: Kuchi Jewelry
description: Heavy silver ornaments of the Kuchi nomadic herders of Afghanistan, such as large necklaces, headpieces and bangles set with amber, carnelian and turquoise. Kuchi jewellery carries the wealth of nomadic families on the move, and its patterns echo ancient Central Asian styles preserved through generations of wandering life across the Afghan plains.
source: Ethnographic documentation of Kuchi material culture

name: Rubab
description: Short-necked plucked lute of Afghanistan, carved from a single block of mulberry wood with a skin belly and three main strings, sounded with a wooden plectrum. The rubab is called the lion of Afghan instruments and leads the classical music of Kabul, its deep drone carrying the folk and court tradition of the region.
material: mulberry wood, animal skin, nylon and steel strings

name: Didgeridoo
description: Long hollowed wooden trumpet of the Aboriginal peoples of northern Australia, made from eucalyptus limbs hollowed by termites and played by vibrating the lips to produce a deep continuous drone. The didgeridoo accompanies song and ceremony, and in northern traditions its sound is held to echo the voices of ancestors and the great Rainbow Serpent, giving music to the Dreaming.
